title: Strive on
hook: the Buddha's last words: all component things decay; work on with diligence
carry: decay is inherent in all component things

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was satipatthana, and the charnel ground's line: this body too is of the same nature. Your line was all bodies. Today, the Buddha's own last night.

Last words get repeated. People write them down, argue over them, carve them on stones. The long discourse on the Buddha's final days ends with his, spoken at night in a grove near a small town called Kusinara, as he lies between two sal trees with his monks gathered close. Earlier, Ananda has gone aside to weep. The last words are not a blessing, not a promise, not a farewell. They are a short sentence of instruction, half fact and half job. The teacher is still teaching.
screen: `A GROVE AT NIGHT, TWO SAL TREES.` → `THE MONKS GATHERED CLOSE.` → `HE IS STILL TEACHING.`

segments.voice: First, no new teacher. Before the end, the Buddha tells Ananda that some may think: the word of the Master is over, we have no teacher anymore. Not so. The teaching and the discipline he has given them will be their teacher after he is gone. Second, any doubts? He asks the monks whether any of them has a doubt or a question about the Buddha, the teaching, the path or the order. Ask now, he says, so you won't regret later that you didn't ask while the teacher was face to face with you. They are silent. He asks a second time, and a third. Silence. Third, the fact. Then the last words. In T. W. Rhys Davids's old translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" The first half is the fact. Everything put together comes apart: bodies, plans, friendships, mountains, the teacher lying in front of them. Nothing in the sentence softens that. Fourth, the job. The second half doesn't say: so despair. It says: so work. The Pali word Rhys Davids renders as diligence is appamada, the heedfulness the Buddha praised in the monks who recalled death with each breath. Other translators put the line more simply: strive on, with heedfulness. Death is not the end of the sentence. Diligence is. In this telling, remembering that things fall apart is a reason to use well the time they hold together.
screen: `THE TEACHING WILL BE YOUR TEACHER.` · `ANY DOUBTS? ASKED THREE TIMES.` · `DECAY IS INHERENT IN ALL COMPONENT THINGS.` · `WORK OUT YOUR SALVATION WITH DILIGENCE.` · then, large: `STRIVE ON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing in your life that's half done, a message, a drawer, a form, a repair, and notice without scolding why it's been waiting: tiredness, dread, distraction. Then hold the first half of the line, everything put together comes apart, and let it make the moment feel a little more precious than urgent.
Strive on: the Buddha's last instruction. All put-together things decay, so work on with diligence and heedfulness. Today's word.
Your line: decay is inherent in all component things. The fact first, then the work. Day seven hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Some Buddhists remember the Buddha's last words, recited in Pali, as a reminder of impermanence and a call to practice with heedfulness rather than delay.

chat.says: What were the Buddha's very last words?
options: All put-together things decay, so work on with diligence.
A blessing promising his monks they'd all reach nibbana soon.
A farewell asking his monks to mourn him for seven days.
chat.meaning: Decay is the fact and diligence is the job: appamada, the heedfulness he praised in the monks who recalled death with each breath.

Kusinara.meaning: the small town near the grove where the Buddha died

sal.meaning: a kind of tree; the Buddha lay between two of them

Rhys Davids.meaning: the scholar whose old English translation is quoted
